summary_en: Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine reshaped European energy security questions, including the role of the (then-paused) Nord Stream 2 pipeline. Kóczy, Sziklai and Csercsik model the European natural-gas market from a supply-security perspective. They combine a linear-programming gas-flow model with the financial-risk concept of Expected Shortfall (ES) to quantify supply-disruption risk. They show that shifting Russian gas exports from Ukraine to Nord Stream 2 increases supply risk for South-Eastern Europe — including Hungary — and that the Trans-Anatolian and Trans-Adriatic Pipelines only partially compensate. Overall, Nord Stream 2 would have reduced Eastern European energy security.
data_used: European natural-gas pipeline network topology and capacity data, 2020-2022; Russian gas-export flow records; supply-disruption scenarios calibrated to actual events. Linear-programming gas-flow model + Expected Shortfall risk metric.
policy_relevance: Direct evidence for Hungarian and EU energy policy. The MEKH (Hungarian Energy Office), MNV (state asset manager), and MFB (Hungarian Development Bank) all engaged with Nord Stream 2 questions. The paper provides quantitative supply-security analysis showing why Eastern European countries should favour pipeline diversification over Nord Stream 2 — a finding vindicated by the 2022 sabotage and Russian gas weaponisation.
title: Nord Stream 2: A prelude to war
